summary: Describes the NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol for signaling Quality of Service reservations. Together with GIST it gives RSVP-like function, independent of the QoS model, without multicast support. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Calling ahead to reserve space on the road for your messages so they arrive on time.

questions: how does qos nslp reservation work
how do routers handle qos reservation changes
what is soft-state in signaling protocols
subtitle: Reserve bandwidth and network resources across the Internet with soft-state signaling.

tldr.problem: Applications need guaranteed bandwidth, low latency, or other quality-of-service properties, but the Internet provides best-effort service. End-to-end QoS requires signaling to every router along the path to install reservations.
tldr.mechanism: The QoS NSLP sends RESERVE messages along the data path. Each router makes policy and admission control decisions, configures its packet scheduler and classifier, and forwards the message. Soft-state ensures old reservations expire. Both sender-initiated and receiver-initiated signaling are supported.
tldr.outcome: Routers can provide QoS to flows that signal their needs. The protocol is QoS-model-agnostic and decouples signaling from specific resource management. It adapts to rerouting and supports flexible reservation patterns.

today: RFC 5974 is an Experimental specification for QoS signaling in the NSIS framework. While NSIS was designed to be more deployable than RSVP, widespread deployment has not occurred. Modern QoS in the Internet typically relies on DiffServ classification (without per-flow signaling) or application-level techniques (e.g., adaptive bitrate video streaming). The QoS NSLP remains a reference design for future QoS signaling systems.

sections.title: The Need for Quality of Service
sections.content:
The Internet delivers data on a best-effort basis: routers forward packets without any guarantees. For real-time applications like voice and video calls, this works poorly when networks are congested. These applications need guaranteed bandwidth, bounded delay, and low jitter to sound and look good.

The solution is Quality of Service (QoS) signaling. Before an application sends data, it tells the network what it needs. Every router along the path makes an admission control decision: is there enough capacity to provide what the application asks for? If yes, the router allocates resources and configures its packet scheduler. If no, the application gets an error and can retry, choose a lower quality, or wait.

The QoS NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol (QoS NSLP) is a way to deliver these requests to every router along the path. It is inspired by RSVP but redesigned as part of the NSIS framework, transported by GIST instead of a custom transport layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending your video, you ask every router on the path: "Can you give my packets priority?" If they all say yes, your video streams smoothly. If any say no, you know it won't work.

sections.title: Core Protocol Concepts
sections.content:
The QoS NSLP uses four message types, each with a specific purpose:

RESERVE messages request, modify, or remove QoS reservations. They are the only messages that change reservation state. Each RESERVE is idempotent: receiving it twice has the same effect as receiving it once.

QUERY messages probe the path to learn what QoS is available or what resources are currently in use, without making a reservation. A router receiving a QUERY responds with information about its capabilities.

RESPONSE messages provide information about the success or failure of a RESERVE or QUERY. They travel back to the sender of the request.

NOTIFY messages are sent asynchronously to inform peers of state changes or errors, such as when a reservation times out or when a higher-priority flow preempts a lower-priority one.

The protocol uses soft-state: reservations expire after a timeout unless refreshed. Refresh messages can use a reduced refresh format that references an existing reservation by its sequence number rather than repeating the full specification, saving bandwidth.

Messages travel peer-to-peer: each QoS node (QNE) sends to its immediate neighbor, not directly to the source or destination. This keeps local control local and prevents any single point of failure.
sections.plainLanguage: RESERVE requests resources. QUERY asks what's available. RESPONSE confirms success or reports failure. NOTIFY tells you about changes. Reservations must be refreshed periodically or they disappear.

sections.title: Sender-Initiated and Receiver-Initiated Signaling
sections.content:
The QoS NSLP supports two patterns of reservation:

Sender-initiated: The sender (QNI) creates a RESERVE message and sends it toward the receiver (QNR). The message travels along the data path. Each router installs a reservation for traffic going toward the receiver. The receiver generates a RESPONSE confirming the reservation is in place.

Receiver-initiated: The receiver determines what QoS it needs and sends a RESERVE message back toward the sender. The router near the receiver installs a reservation for traffic coming from the sender. The sender responds with a RESPONSE.

Receiver-initiated signaling is useful when the sender does not know the receiver's requirements in advance, or when the receiver must decide based on its capabilities. For example, a video player could query the network path first with a QUERY message to learn what bandwidth is available, then the sender could make a RESERVE matching that capacity.

Both patterns can operate together for bidirectional flows: a RESERVE from the sender reserves the forward direction, and a RESERVE from the receiver reserves the reverse direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Sender-initiated: "I'm sending video; please prioritize it." Receiver-initiated: "Please prioritize traffic to me." Both can happen for two-way calls.

sections.title: Resource Management and QoS Models
sections.content:
The QoS NSLP separates signaling from resource management. The protocol defines how messages flow, but not what happens when they arrive at a router. That is the job of a Resource Management Function (RMF), specific to each QoS model.

The RMF at each router reads the QSPEC object in the RESERVE message. This is an opaque container of QoS parameters—bandwidth in bits per second, maximum delay, maximum jitter, and so on. The RMF interprets these according to its local QoS model (which could be IntServ, DiffServ, or something else entirely). It makes an admission control decision: do we have enough resources?

If yes, the RMF configures the router's packet classifier and packet scheduler to treat matching traffic with the promised QoS. It passes a success response back.

If no, the RMF rejects the request and returns an error, allowing the application to try again with lower QoS requirements.

This design allows the same NSLP to work with different QoS models. A network can implement IntServ, DiffServ, or a proprietary model without changing the signaling protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The signaling protocol just carries a request. Local routers read the request and decide how to actually provide the promised quality. Different routers can use different methods.

sections.title: Handling Route Changes and Rerouting
sections.content:
When a router reroutes traffic to a different next hop due to a link failure or network change, the QoS reservation must be updated for the new path. The QoS NSLP detects this by observing when the next QNE peer changes (indicated by GIST). When a RESERVE arrives from a different neighbor than previously, the local QNE knows rerouting has occurred.

The QNE sends a new RESERVE message down the new path with full specifications (QSPEC included). Routers on the new path install new reservations. Once the new path is confirmed with a RESPONSE, the QNE can optionally tear down the old reservation by sending a tearing RESERVE down the old path.

A REPLACE flag in the common header indicates whether to keep reservations on old branches. This is useful in mobile networks where keeping an old path is cheaper than repeatedly tearing down and reinstalling.

Sequence numbers (RSN) protect against duplicate and reordered messages. When rerouting occurs, RSN numbering uses a special scheme to avoid accidentally tearing down a reserved path that is still useful.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router detects the path changed, it tells the next router the whole requirements again. Once confirmed, it cleans up the old path (unless it wants to keep it as a backup).

sections.title: Advanced Features: Aggregation, Layering, and Policy
sections.content:
Aggregate reservations combine multiple individual flows under a single reservation to reduce signaling overhead. For example, a network edge can make one large reservation toward a destination for all flows going there, rather than reserving each flow separately. The QoS NSLP supports this by binding an end-to-end session to an aggregate session using a BOUND-SESSION-ID object.

Layering supports scenarios where domains have different QoS models or signaling policies. A domain can establish a local session using its internal QoS model and bind it to an end-to-end session that passes through unchanged. Intermediate routers that do not support QoS can be bypassed by higher-level router alert options.

Policy control ensures only authorized applications get QoS. Each QNE consults with a policy decision point (AAA infrastructure) to decide if the requester is allowed to reserve resources. GIST channel security authenticates neighbors, and authorization tokens from external protocols (like SIP) can be attached to RESERVE messages.

Preemption allows higher-priority flows to displace lower-priority ones when resources are exhausted. The QoS NSLP provides information objects to signal preemption, but the RMF controls the actual behavior per QoS model.
sections.plainLanguage: Multiple flows can be bundled into one big reservation. Different parts of the network can use different methods. Only authorized applications get QoS. Important traffic can kick out less important traffic if needed.
